reasoning: The exponents add: p^2/(qr)+q^2/(rp)+r^2/(pq) = (p^3+q^3+r^3)/(pqr). With p+q+r=0 we have p^3+q^3+r^3=3pqr, so the exponent is 3. Confirmed symbolically (substituting r=-p-q gives exactly 3) and on three asymmetric numeric triples (2,3,-5), (5,-1,-4), (1/3,7,-22/3), each giving 3.
solution: The three powers of \(z\) multiply, so the exponents add to \(\frac{p^3+q^3+r^3}{pqr}\). Because \(p+q+r=0\) forces \(p^3+q^3+r^3=3pqr\), that exponent equals \(3\). The product is therefore \(z^3\).

reasoning: An identity in x requires every coefficient to vanish. k^2-5k+4=0 gives k in {1,4}; k^2-3k-4=0 gives k in {4,-1}; k^2-4k=0 gives k in {0,4}. The single common value is 4.
solution: For the equation to be an identity every coefficient must vanish at the same value of \(k\). Now \(k^2-5k+4=0\) gives \(k=1\) or \(4\), \(k^2-3k-4=0\) gives \(k=4\) or \(-1\), and \(k^2-4k=0\) gives \(k=0\) or \(4\). Only \(k=4\) satisfies all three.

reasoning: Set each ratio equal to t; adding numerators and denominators gives a^2+b^2+c^2 = 2t(a^2+b^2+c^2), so t=1/2 and 2a^2=b^2+c^2 with its two companions. Subtracting these in pairs forces a^2=b^2=c^2; sympy confirms b=a, c=a is the only positive solution of the system. Then a^4+b^4+c^4 = 3a^4 = a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2, so the multiplier is 1.
solution: Calling the common ratio \(t\) and adding the three numerators and the three denominators gives \(a^2+b^2+c^2=2t(a^2+b^2+c^2)\), so \(t=\tfrac12\) and \(2a^2=b^2+c^2\) along with its two companions. Subtracting those in pairs forces \(a^2=b^2=c^2\). Both \(a^4+b^4+c^4\) and \(a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2\) then equal \(3a^4\), so the value is \(a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2\).

reasoning: 1/x = 1/p + 1/q gives x = pq/(p+q). Then (x+p)/(x-p) = -(p+2q)/p and (x+q)/(x-q) = -(q+2p)/q, whose difference is 2(p^2-q^2)/(pq); multiplying by pq/(p^2-q^2) leaves 2. sympy simplifies the whole expression to 2.
solution: From \(\frac1x=\frac1p+\frac1q\) we get \(x=\frac{pq}{p+q}\), which makes \(\frac{x+p}{x-p}=-\frac{p+2q}{p}\) and \(\frac{x+q}{x-q}=-\frac{q+2p}{q}\). Their difference simplifies to \(\frac{2(p^2-q^2)}{pq}\). Multiplying by \(\frac{pq}{p^2-q^2}\) leaves \(2\).

reasoning: Every factor of P (5, 15, 25, 35) is odd, so P is odd; every factor of Q (10, 20, 30, 40) is even, so Q is even. Odd + even is odd, and an odd number cannot end in 0. Computed directly: P+Q ends in the digit 5 with 0 trailing zeros.
solution: Each factor making up \(P\) is odd, so \(P\) is odd, while every factor making up \(Q\) is even, so \(Q\) is even. Their sum is therefore odd, and an odd number cannot end in \(0\). The number of consecutive zeros at the end is zero.

reasoning: x-5 divides both, so x=5 is a root of each. 25-5-p=0 gives p=20; 25-5q-10=0 gives q=3. Then p+q=23. Check: x^2-x-20=(x-5)(x+4) and x^2-3x-10=(x-5)(x+2), whose HCF is indeed x-5.
solution: Because \(x-5\) divides both polynomials, \(x=5\) is a root of each. From \(25-5-p=0\) we get \(p=20\), and from \(25-5q-10=0\) we get \(q=3\). Hence \(p+q=23\), and the two polynomials factor as \((x-5)(x+4)\) and \((x-5)(x+2)\), confirming the HCF.

reasoning: LCM x HCF = p(x) q(x). Here LCM x HCF = (x+a)(x-a)(x^2+ax+a^2)(x^2-ax+a^2) = (x^2-a^2)(x^4+a^2x^2+a^4), so q(x) = x^2-a^2. No other option satisfies the product relation. NOTE the stem is internally inconsistent: p(x)=(x^2+ax+a^2)(x^2-ax+a^2) and x^2-a^2 have gcd 1 (sympy confirms), so no pair actually has HCF x^2-ax+a^2, and the stated LCM is not a multiple of p(x). Option C is nevertheless forced by the only relation available.
solution: Using \(\text{LCM}\times\text{HCF}=p(x)\,q(x)\), the left side is \((x+a)(x^3-a^3)(x^2-ax+a^2)=(x^2-a^2)(x^4+a^2x^2+a^4)\). Dividing by \(p(x)=x^4+a^2x^2+a^4\) leaves \(q(x)=x^2-a^2\). The question is defective in one respect: \(p(x)=(x^2+ax+a^2)(x^2-ax+a^2)\) and \(x^2-a^2\) share no common factor, so no pair of polynomials really has the stated HCF.

reasoning: Both cubics vanish at x=1. At x=-1 the first gives 8 and the second -4, so x+1 divides neither. At x=-2 the first gives 12 while the second vanishes, so x+2 divides only the second. sympy gives gcd = x-1.
solution: Both cubics vanish at \(x=1\), so \(x-1\) divides each of them. At \(x=-1\) the first gives \(8\), so \(x+1\) divides neither; at \(x=-2\) the first gives \(12\) while the second vanishes, so \(x+2\) divides only the second. Only the first expression divides both.

reasoning: 8m+24w=1 and 12m+18w=1 give 6w=4m, so m=1.5w and 36w=1, i.e. w=1/36 and m=1/24. Then 24m+72w = 1+2 = 3 jobs per day, so the time is 1/3 day.
solution: Both crews finish in one day, so \(8m+24w=1\) and \(12m+18w=1\), which give \(6w=4m\) and hence \(m=\tfrac1{24}\), \(w=\tfrac1{36}\) of the work per day. Then \(24\) men and \(72\) women complete \(24m+72w=3\) such jobs in a day. The work therefore takes \(\tfrac13\) of a day.

reasoning: No solution needs k/(-12) = -5/(4(k-1)), i.e. 4k^2-4k-60=0 or k^2-k-15=0, with discriminant 61. The roots (1 +/- sqrt 61)/2 are irrational. A sweep of every integer k from -20 to 20 finds none making the pair inconsistent.
solution: The system has no solution when the coefficients of \(x\) and \(y\) are proportional but the constants are not, i.e. \(\frac{k}{-12}=\frac{-5}{4(k-1)}\). This reduces to \(k^2-k-15=0\), whose discriminant is \(61\), not a perfect square. The roots \(\frac{1\pm\sqrt{61}}{2}\) are irrational, so no integral value of \(k\) works.

reasoning: 7(10a+b)=4(10b+a) gives 66a=33b, i.e. b=2a. With b<=9 this allows a=1,2,3,4. A direct sweep of all two-digit numbers finds exactly 12, 24, 36, 48.
solution: Writing the number as \(10a+b\), the condition \(7(10a+b)=4(10b+a)\) reduces to \(66a=33b\), that is \(b=2a\). Since \(b\le 9\), this allows \(a=1,2,3,4\), giving \(12, 24, 36\) and \(48\). There are \(4\) such numbers.

reasoning: 12% per annum compounded quarterly is 3% per quarter. 3300 x 1.03 = 3399 exactly, so one quarter suffices. Later quarters give 3500.97, 3606.00, 3714.18, none equal to 3399.
solution: Compounded quarterly at \(12\%\) per annum, the rate is \(3\%\) per quarter, so after one quarter the amount is \(3300\times1.03=3399\). That is reached in exactly one quarter, namely \(3\) months.

reasoning: With x=ky: x^2+y^2 = (k^2+1)y^2, a constant multiple of y^2, so I holds. x^3/y^4 = k^3/y, which varies inversely as y, so II fails.
solution: Direct variation means \(x=ky\) for a constant \(k\). Then \(x^2+y^2=(k^2+1)y^2\), which is a fixed multiple of \(y^2\), so the first statement holds. But \(\frac{x^3}{y^4}=\frac{k^3}{y}\), which varies inversely as \(y\) rather than directly, so the second fails.

reasoning: Rates 1/4 and 1/6 per day. Starting with X, four days give 1/4+1/6+1/4+1/6 = 5/6, and X clears the remaining 1/6 in 2/3 of day five, so the work finishes on the fifth day: I holds. Starting with Y, four days also give 5/6, and Y's fifth-day share is exactly 1/6, so it takes a full 5 days, not less than 5: II fails. Simulated exactly with fractions.
solution: X completes \(\tfrac14\) and Y completes \(\tfrac16\) of the work per day. Starting with X, the first four days give \(\tfrac14+\tfrac16+\tfrac14+\tfrac16=\tfrac56\), and X clears the remaining \(\tfrac16\) in \(\tfrac23\) of the fifth day, so the work does finish on the fifth day. Starting with Y the first four days also give \(\tfrac56\), but Y's fifth-day share is exactly \(\tfrac16\), so the work takes a full five days rather than less, and only the first statement is correct.

reasoning: Volumes are 100 x 0.20 x 5 = 100 m^3 and 200 x 0.60 x 5 = 600 m^3, a ratio of 6. The first needs 12 x 8 x 10 = 960 man-hours, so the second needs 5760. At 16 x 10 = 160 man-hours per day that is 36 days.
solution: The two walls measure \(100\times0.2\times5=100\) m\(^3\) and \(200\times0.6\times5=600\) m\(^3\), a ratio of \(6\). The first takes \(12\times8\times10=960\) man-hours, so the second needs \(5760\) man-hours. At \(16\times10=160\) man-hours a day that is \(36\) days.

reasoning: If they meet after time t, then P covers in t what Q covers in 1 hour and Q covers in t what P covers in 4 hours: Vp t = Vq and Vq t = 4 Vp. Multiplying gives t^2 = 4, t = 2, so Vq = 2 Vp = 120 km/h. sympy returns Vq=120, t=2.
solution: If the trains meet after time \(t\), then the stretch \(P\) has covered is what \(Q\) still covers in \(1\) hour and vice versa, giving \(V_Pt=V_Q\) and \(V_Qt=4V_P\). Multiplying the two gives \(t^2=4\), so \(t=2\). Hence \(V_Q=2V_P=120\) km/h.

reasoning: In one hour with stoppages the train covers 48 km; at 60 km/h that distance takes 48/60 hour = 48 minutes of running. The remaining 12 minutes of the hour are spent stopped.
solution: In one hour the train with stoppages covers \(48\) km, and at \(60\) km/h that distance takes \(\frac{48}{60}\) hour, i.e. \(48\) minutes of actual running. The remaining \(12\) minutes of each hour are spent stopped.

reasoning: Downstream speed b+w = x and upstream b-w = y, so b=(x+y)/2 and w=(x-y)/2, and their ratio is (x+y)/(x-y).
solution: Downstream the boat and the current add, and upstream they subtract, so \(b+w=x\) and \(b-w=y\). Solving gives the boat's still-water speed \(\frac{x+y}{2}\) and the current's speed \(\frac{x-y}{2}\). Their ratio is \(\frac{x+y}{x-y}\).

reasoning: Sum of roots -b equals product c, so c=-b and Q=x^2+bx-b with discriminant b^2+4b. That vanishes at b=0 and b=-4, giving Q=x^2 and Q=(x-2)^2, so I holds. II is a universal claim and fails: at b=0, Q=x^2 is zero at x=0, and at b=1, Q=x^2+x-1 equals -1 at x=0. RUNNER-UP: option C, which would win if II were read existentially ('Q can be positive for all x'), true for -4<b<0; but II is phrased as a statement about Q, not about some Q.
solution: The sum of the roots is \(-b\) and the product is \(c\), so \(c=-b\) and \(Q=x^2+bx-b\) with discriminant \(b^2+4b\). This vanishes at \(b=0\) and \(b=-4\), giving \(Q=x^2\) and \(Q=(x-2)^2\), so \(Q\) can indeed be a perfect square. It need not be positive everywhere, however: \(x^2\) is zero at \(x=0\) and \(x^2+x-1\) is negative there, so only the first statement is correct.

reasoning: Writing the ages 4t and 5t, (4t-k)/(5t-k)=1/2 gives 3t=k. Both ages are whole numbers, and since 5t-4t=t, t must itself be a positive integer, so k is a multiple of 3. With k<10 that leaves k=3,6,9. Exhaustive search over k=1..9 confirms exactly these three, with ages (4,5),(8,10),(12,15).
solution: Writing the present ages as \(4t\) and \(5t\), the condition \(\frac{4t-k}{5t-k}=\frac12\) reduces to \(3t=k\). Since both ages are whole numbers and their difference is \(t\), the value \(t\) must be a positive integer, so \(k\) is a multiple of \(3\). With \(k<10\) that gives \(k=3, 6, 9\), corresponding to ages \((4,5)\), \((8,10)\) and \((12,15)\), so \(3\) values are possible.

reasoning: 27^27 - 9^40 - 3^79 = 3^81 - 3^80 - 3^79 = 3^79(9-3-1) = 5 x 3^79, verified by direct integer computation. Among 1..9 it is divisible by 1, 3, 5 and 9 only, so four numbers, i.e. more than three.
solution: Writing everything in powers of three, \(27^{27}-9^{40}-3^{79}=3^{81}-3^{80}-3^{79}=3^{79}(9-3-1)=5\times3^{79}\). Being odd it is divisible by no even number, and it is not a multiple of \(7\). Among the natural numbers below \(10\) it is divisible by \(1, 3, 5\) and \(9\), which is more than three.

reasoning: gcd(p, p+q) = gcd(p, q) = G and gcd(p, p-q) = gcd(p, q) = G by the Euclidean property. A sweep over all pairs with p up to 120 finds no counterexample to either statement.
solution: The Euclidean property gives \(\gcd(p, p+q)=\gcd(p,q)\) and \(\gcd(p, p-q)=\gcd(p,q)\), since adding or subtracting a multiple of one argument leaves the HCF unchanged. Both HCFs therefore equal \(G\), so both statements are correct.

reasoning: p = 55 x 4 = 220. Since pq = HCF x LCM = 44 x 4620 = 203280, q = 924. Check: gcd(220,924)=44 and lcm=4620, both matching the stem.
solution: Dividing by \(55\) with quotient \(4\) and remainder \(0\) gives \(p=220\). Since the product of two numbers equals the product of their HCF and LCM, \(220\,q=44\times4620=203280\), so \(q=924\). Checking back, \(\gcd(220, 924)=44\) and their LCM is \(4620\).

reasoning: A number leaving the same remainder on all three must divide the pairwise differences 31, 93 and 124, whose gcd is 31. Each of 600, 631, 724 leaves remainder 11 on division by 31.
solution: A divisor leaving the same remainder on all three numbers must divide their differences \(631-600=31\), \(724-631=93\) and \(724-600=124\). The greatest such number is \(\gcd(31, 93, 124)=31\), and indeed each of the three leaves remainder \(11\).

reasoning: Scaling by 1000 gives 3600, 9, 270 with LCM 2^4 x 3^3 x 5^2 = 10800, so the LCM of the decimals is 10.8. Checked with exact fractions: 10.8 is an exact multiple of all three, and 5.4 and 16.2 are not (21.6 is a common multiple but not the least).
solution: Multiplying all three by \(1000\) gives \(3600, 9\) and \(270\), whose LCM is \(2^4\times3^3\times5^2=10800\). Dividing back by \(1000\) gives \(10.8\), which is an exact multiple of \(3.6\), \(0.009\) and \(0.27\), and no smaller positive number is.

reasoning: The speed must divide both distances exactly, so the greatest is HCF(13.3, 20.9). Scaling by 10, gcd(133, 209) = 19 since 133 = 7 x 19 and 209 = 11 x 19. At 1.9 km/h the times are exactly 7 and 11 hours.
solution: For both times to be whole numbers the speed must divide both distances exactly, so the greatest such speed is the HCF of \(13.3\) and \(20.9\). Scaling by \(10\), \(133=7\times19\) and \(209=11\times19\), so the HCF is \(19\) and the speed is \(1.9\) km/h. The journeys then take exactly \(7\) and \(11\) hours.

reasoning: 256 = 2^8, so the divisors are 1, 2, 4, ..., 256 and their sum is 2^9 - 1 = 511. Direct summation confirms 511.
solution: Since \(256=2^8\), its divisors are \(1, 2, 4, \ldots, 256\), a geometric progression. Their sum is \(2^9-1=511\).

reasoning: Consecutive naturals differ by 1, so any common divisor divides 1 and they are co-prime: I holds. II fails at m=3, n=5, which are relatively prime while mn=15 is odd.
solution: Two consecutive natural numbers differ by \(1\), so any common divisor must divide \(1\) and they are always co-prime. The second statement fails at \(m=3\) and \(n=5\), which are relatively prime while \(m\times n=15\) is odd. Only the first statement is correct.

reasoning: p = 3 log2 + 1, q = 2 log3 + 1 - log2, r = 3 log2 + 3 log3. Then p - q + r = 7 log2 + log3 = log(2^7 x 3) = log 384. Numerically p-q+r = 2.584331224 matches log 384 exactly, while the other three combinations give 5.8908, -2.0846 and 1.2218.
solution: Writing everything in \(\log 2\) and \(\log 3\): \(p=3\log 2+1\), \(q=2\log 3+1-\log 2\) and \(r=3\log 2+3\log 3\). Then \(p-q+r=7\log 2+\log 3\). Since \(384=2^7\times3\), this is exactly \(\log_{10}384\).

reasoning: All five factors are odd, so the product is odd, and the factor 5^5 makes it a multiple of 5. An odd multiple of 5 ends in 5. Direct computation of the product mod 10 gives 5.
solution: Every factor in the product is odd, so the product itself is odd, and the factor \(5^5\) makes it a multiple of \(5\). An odd multiple of \(5\) must end in \(5\), so the units digit is \(5\).

reasoning: N = 2m+1 gives N^2 = 4m(m+1)+1, and m(m+1) is even so 8 divides 4m(m+1). Remainder is always 1; checking every odd N from -101 to 101 gives the residue set {1}.
solution: Writing \(N=2m+1\) gives \(N^2=4m(m+1)+1\), and \(m(m+1)\) is a product of consecutive integers, hence even. So \(8\) divides \(4m(m+1)\) and the remainder is always \(1\), whatever odd integer \(N\) is.

reasoning: With original price P, 2790/(0.9P) - 2790/P = 6.2 reduces to 2790/(9P) = 6.2, giving P = 50. The reduced price is 0.9 x 50 = 45. sympy returns P = 50.
solution: If the original price is \(P\) rupees per kilogram, the extra quantity bought is \(\frac{2790}{0.9P}-\frac{2790}{P}=6.2\), which simplifies to \(\frac{2790}{9P}=6.2\) and gives \(P=50\). The reduced price is \(0.9\times50=45\) rupees per kilogram.

reasoning: Successive discounts leave (1-p/100)(1-p/200)(1-p/400) = 0.684. sympy gives the positive root p = 20, and 0.8 x 0.9 x 0.95 = 0.684 exactly.
solution: Three successive discounts leave a factor \(\left(1-\frac{p}{100}\right)\left(1-\frac{p}{200}\right)\left(1-\frac{p}{400}\right)\), which must equal \(1-0.316=0.684\). At \(p=20\) this is \(0.8\times0.9\times0.95=0.684\) exactly, so \(p=20\%\).

reasoning: Speed = 40 - c sqrt(n). With n=36, 40-6c=16 gives c=4, so speed = 40 - 4 sqrt(n). This is zero at n=100 and negative beyond, so the engine cannot move once n >= 100; the smallest such number is 100.
solution: The reduction is \(c\sqrt{n}\), and \(40-6c=16\) gives \(c=4\), so the speed is \(40-4\sqrt{n}\). The engine cannot move once this ceases to be positive, that is once \(\sqrt{n}\ge10\). The smallest such number of wagons is \(100\).

reasoning: (P+1)/(Q+1)=7/10 and (P+3)/(Q+3)=3/4 give P=6, Q=9, so x:y = 2:3. The quantity (x+y)/(x-y) is invariant under scaling the ratio: 5/(-1) = -5 for x=2,y=3 and 15/(-3) = -5 for x=6,y=9.
solution: From \(\frac{P+1}{Q+1}=\frac7{10}\) and \(\frac{P+3}{Q+3}=\frac34\) we get \(10P-7Q=-3\) and \(4P-3Q=-3\), so \(P=6\) and \(Q=9\), i.e. \(x:y=2:3\). Then \(\frac{x+y}{x-y}=\frac{5}{-1}=-5\), and this value does not change if the ratio is written in any other equivalent form.

reasoning: Right angle at C gives AC = sqrt(100-64) = 6, so CP = AP - AC = 10 - 6 = 4. Since P is on AC produced, angle BCP is also a right angle, so BP = sqrt(64+16) = sqrt 80 = 4 sqrt 5 = 8.944 cm. The semicircle on AB is incidental to this computation.
solution: The right angle at \(C\) gives \(AC=\sqrt{10^2-8^2}=6\) cm, so \(CP=AP-AC=10-6=4\) cm. Since \(P\) lies on \(AC\) produced, angle \(BCP\) is also a right angle. Hence \(BP=\sqrt{8^2+4^2}=\sqrt{80}=4\sqrt5\) cm.

reasoning: There are C(5,3)=10 groups and each letter appears in C(4,2)=6 of them, so the aggregate is 6(A+B+C+D+E)=120. The total is 20 and the mean is 4.
solution: There are \(\binom{5}{3}=10\) groups, and each of the five numbers appears in \(\binom{4}{2}=6\) of them. So the aggregate of the group sums is \(6(A+B+C+D+E)=120\), giving a total of \(20\) and an arithmetic mean of \(4\).

reasoning: Adding a constant to every observation shifts the mean by the same constant: 50 + 10 = 60.
solution: Adding the same constant to every observation shifts the mean by exactly that constant. The new arithmetic mean is \(50+10=60\).

reasoning: Sum(x_i) - 15n = -90 and Sum(x_i) + 3n = 54. Subtracting gives 18n = 144, so n = 8 and Sum(x_i) = 30, mean = 30/8 = 3.75. sympy returns n=8, S=30.
solution: The two conditions give \(\sum x_i-15n=-90\) and \(\sum x_i+3n=54\). Subtracting the first from the second gives \(18n=144\), so \(n=8\) and \(\sum x_i=30\). The arithmetic mean is \(\frac{30}{8}=3.75\).

reasoning: With twelve terms the median is the mean of the sixth and seventh, which are 8x+1 and x^2+1; setting that to 25 gives x^2+8x-48=0 with roots 4 and -12. x=-12 fails on BOTH readings: as written the list becomes 59,53,51,43,36,-95,145,13,... which is not descending, and re-sorting it gives median (36+13)/2 = 24.5, not 25. x=4 gives 33 and 17 in those slots, keeping the list descending with median 25. RUNNER-UP: option C, which is what solving the median equation alone yields if the descending-order condition is not checked.
solution: With twelve values in descending order the median is the mean of the sixth and seventh, so \(\frac{(8x+1)+(x^2+1)}{2}=25\), that is \(x^2+8x-48=0\) with roots \(x=4\) and \(x=-12\). Only \(x=4\) survives, giving \(33\) and \(17\) in those two places and keeping the list descending. Taking \(x=-12\) puts \(-95\) and \(145\) there, which breaks the stated order and, even after re-sorting, gives a median of \(24.5\).

reasoning: The left side combines to 2 cos t/(1 - sin^2 t) = 2/cos t = 4, so cos t = 1/2 and sin^2 t = 3/4. Then tan^2 t = 3 and cot^2 t = 1/3, summing to 10/3.
solution: Combining the two fractions gives \(\frac{2\cos\theta}{1-\sin^2\theta}=\frac{2}{\cos\theta}\), so \(\frac{2}{\cos\theta}=4\) and \(\cos\theta=\tfrac12\). Then \(\tan^2\theta=3\) and \(\cot^2\theta=\tfrac13\), so their sum is \(\frac{10}{3}\).

value: Both I and II are identities
reasoning: I factors as tan^4 t (1+tan^2 t) x cot^4 t (1+cot^2 t) = sec^2 t cosec^2 t, since tan^4 t cot^4 t = 1. For II, (tan t + sin t)/(tan t - sin t) = (1+cos t)/(1-cos t) and cot^2 t (sec t + 1)^2 = (1+cos t)^2/sin^2 t, which equals the same. Checked at 40-digit precision at theta = 0.05, 0.31, 0.73, 1.19, 1.45 radians (deliberately not 30, 45 or 60 degrees); both hold at every point.
solution: The first factorises as \(\tan^4\theta(1+\tan^2\theta)\cdot\cot^4\theta(1+\cot^2\theta)\), and since \(\tan^4\theta\cot^4\theta=1\) this is \(\sec^2\theta\,\mathrm{cosec}^2\theta\). For the second, \(\frac{\tan\theta+\sin\theta}{\tan\theta-\sin\theta}=\frac{1+\cos\theta}{1-\cos\theta}\), while \(\cot^2\theta(\sec\theta+1)^2=\frac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{\sin^2\theta}\) reduces to the same expression. Both are identities.

reasoning: 3 sin t + 4 cos t has maximum 5, so equality forces sin t = 3/5, cos t = 4/5 (sympy returns this as the unique solution with sin^2+cos^2=1). Then 4 tan t + 3 cot t = 4(3/4) + 3(4/3) = 3 + 4 = 7.
solution: Since \(3\sin\theta+4\cos\theta\) can be written as \(5\sin(\theta+\phi)\), its maximum value is \(5\), so equality forces \(\sin\theta=\tfrac35\) and \(\cos\theta=\tfrac45\). Then \(\tan\theta=\tfrac34\) and \(\cot\theta=\tfrac43\), giving \(4\tan\theta+3\cot\theta=3+4=7\).

reasoning: h/d = 5/6 and h/(d-70) = 9/8 give d = 6h/5 and d - 70 = 8h/9, so 6h/5 - 8h/9 = 70, i.e. 14h/45 = 70 and h = 225 (with d = 270). sympy confirms h=225, d=270.
solution: If the tower is \(h\) metres high and the first point is \(d\) metres away, then \(\frac hd=\frac56\) and \(\frac{h}{d-70}=\frac98\), so \(d=\frac{6h}{5}\) and \(d-70=\frac{8h}{9}\). Eliminating \(d\) gives \(\frac{6h}{5}-\frac{8h}{9}=70\), that is \(\frac{14h}{45}=70\). Hence \(h=225\) m.
